principles: Danger – Response – Send for help (108/112) – Airway – Breathing – CPR – Defibrillation. Use it in every emergency; your own safety first.
Life threats in order: catastrophic bleeding → airway → breathing → circulation → disability (consciousness) → exposure/environment.
Call 108/112 before starting CPR if alone with an adult; send a runner to guide the ambulance to the exact gate.
Unconscious but breathing: on the side, head tilted back, mouth downward, knee bent to stabilise; monitor breathing every minute.
Introduce yourself; get consent from a conscious casualty; record time, findings, treatment, vital signs; hand over using MIST (Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment).
Gloves, barrier mask/face shield for breaths, sharps in containers, hand hygiene; needle-stick: wash, report, post-exposure protocol.

recognise: Unresponsive and not breathing normally (gasping = not breathing)
Check ≤ 10 seconds
do: Call 108/112, send for the AED
30 chest compressions: centre of chest, 5–6 cm deep, 100–120/min, full recoil; then 2 breaths (1 s each, chest rise) — ratio 30:2
Hands-only CPR if unable/unwilling to give breaths
AED as soon as it arrives: switch on, follow voice prompts, attach pads to bare dry chest, nobody touches during analysis/shock, resume CPR immediately after
Continue until the casualty breathes normally, help takes over, or you are exhausted; swap rescuers every 2 min
dont: Don't delay compressions to find a pulse
Don't stop to check unless the casualty moves/breathes
topics.hospital: Always — every arrest goes to hospital by ambulance

recognise: Unresponsive, not breathing normally
do: Child (1 yr–puberty): 5 initial rescue breaths, then 30:2 (15:2 with two trained rescuers); compress 1/3 chest depth (~5 cm) with one or two hands
Infant (< 1 yr): 5 initial breaths, then 30:2 (15:2 two rescuers); two fingers or two-thumb encircling, 4 cm depth; cover mouth and nose with your mouth
If alone, do 1 min of CPR before calling 108 (unless a phone is at hand)
AED with paediatric pads/mode if available; adult pads if not (child > 1 yr)
dont: Don't use abdominal thrusts on infants (choking)
topics.hospital: Always

recognise: Clutching throat, cannot speak/cough/breathe, cyanosis
do: Mild (can cough): encourage coughing; stay with them
Severe adult/child: 5 back blows between shoulder blades (heel of hand), then 5 abdominal thrusts (fist above navel, pull inward and upward); alternate 5 and 5
Infant: 5 back blows (face down along forearm) then 5 chest thrusts (two fingers); no abdominal thrusts
Unresponsive: start CPR; check mouth before breaths and remove visible objects
dont: Don't do blind finger sweeps
topics.hospital: After abdominal thrusts (internal injury check) or if symptoms persist

recognise: Spurting/pooling blood, soaked dressings, pale/cold/clammy, confusion
do: Gloves; expose the wound; apply firm direct pressure with a sterile pad; if it soaks through, add more on top — don't remove
Limb life-threatening bleed not controlled by pressure: apply a tourniquet 5–7 cm above the wound (not over a joint), tighten until bleeding stops, note the time, do not loosen
Junctional wounds (groin/armpit/neck): pack the wound with haemostatic or plain gauze and hold pressure ≥ 3 min
Lay the casualty down, raise legs, keep warm (shock); nothing by mouth
Embedded objects: do not remove; pad around them
dont: Don't apply a tourniquet for minor bleeding
Don't remove the first dressing
topics.hospital: Always for severe bleeding, tourniquet use, or embedded objects

recognise: Pale, cold, clammy skin; rapid weak pulse; fast breathing; thirst; dizziness; confusion; collapse
do: Treat the cause (bleeding, burns, allergic reaction)
Lay flat; raise legs 20–30 cm if no injury prevents; loosen tight clothing; keep warm (blanket under and over)
Reassure; monitor breathing and response every few minutes; recovery position if unconscious
Call 108
dont: Don't give food or drink
Don't apply direct heat
topics.hospital: Always

recognise: Swelling of face/lips/tongue, wheeze/difficulty breathing, hives, collapse after sting, food, drug or chemical exposure
do: Call 108
Adrenaline auto-injector (0.5 mg IM, outer thigh, adult) if the casualty has one or the OHC stocks it; repeat after 5 min if no improvement
Lie flat with legs raised; sit up if breathing is difficult; do not stand them up suddenly
CPR if unresponsive and not breathing
dont: Don't wait to see if it improves
topics.hospital: Always, even after improvement (rebound reactions)

recognise: Central chest pressure/pain spreading to arm/jaw/back, sweating, nausea, breathlessness; may be mild in diabetics/women
do: Call 108; keep calm and rested in a half-sitting 'W' position
If available and not allergic/bleeding risk: chew one aspirin 300 mg (or as advised by the ambulance)
Assist with their own prescribed nitrate spray/tablet if they have it
AED on standby; CPR if they collapse
dont: Don't let them walk or drive
topics.hospital: Always, by ambulance

recognise: FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 108; also sudden confusion, vision loss, severe headache, loss of balance
do: Call 108 immediately; note the time symptoms started (treatment is time-critical)
Keep comfortable, head and shoulders slightly raised; recovery position if unconscious
Reassure; loosen clothing; monitor breathing
dont: Nothing by mouth (swallowing may be affected)
topics.hospital: Always, stroke-ready hospital

recognise: Red, blistered, charred or white/leathery skin; pain (may be absent in deep burns)
do: Stop the burning (stop-drop-roll; smother flames); remove from steam/heat
Cool with cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes — effective up to 3 hours after the burn
Remove clothing, watches, rings not stuck to the skin
Cover loosely with cling film (lengthwise) or a clean non-fluffy dressing; keep the casualty warm
Bitumen/molten metal: cool, leave the material on the skin, cover; hospital will remove
dont: No ice, butter, toothpaste, ointments, cotton wool
Don't burst blisters
Don't cool large burns so long that the casualty becomes cold (hypothermia risk)
topics.hospital: Burn larger than the casualty's palm, any full-thickness burn, burns to face/hands/feet/genitals/joints, circumferential burns, inhalation (smoke, hoarse voice), electrical or chemical burns, children

recognise: Pain, redness, blistering after contact; eye pain, redness, watering, inability to open
do: Protect yourself (gloves, goggles); brush off dry powder before wetting
Remove contaminated clothing while flushing
Flush with copious running water ≥ 20 min (alkalis and HF longer); eyes: hold lids open, flush from the nose outward for ≥ 15–20 min and continue en route to hospital; remove contact lenses
Hydrofluoric acid: after flushing, apply 2.5% calcium gluconate gel and massage continuously; hospital urgently (even small HF burns can be fatal)
Take the SDS/label with the casualty
dont: Don't neutralise with other chemicals
Don't delay flushing to find the SDS
topics.hospital: All chemical eye injuries; HF, phenol, strong acid/alkali burns; any burn larger than a coin

recognise: Contact with electricity; burns at entry/exit; unconsciousness; irregular pulse; muscle pain
do: Isolate the supply first; for LV use a dry non-conductive object to separate; HT – stay ≥ 10 m away and wait for isolation
Check response/breathing; CPR/AED immediately if not breathing
Cool and cover burns; treat shock; immobilise if fallen
dont: Don't touch the casualty while in contact with the source
Don't assume a 'minor' shock is harmless
topics.hospital: All shocks from mains/HT: cardiac monitoring; all electrical burns

recognise: Pain, swelling, deformity, loss of function, grating; spinal: neck/back pain, numbness/tingling, weakness after a fall or high-energy impact
do: Keep still; support the injured part in the position found (hands, padding, splint to the body or adjacent limb)
Open fracture: cover with a sterile dressing; control bleeding without pressing on bone
Check circulation beyond the injury (colour, warmth, pulse) before and after splinting

Suspected spinal injury: do not move unless in danger or airway at risk; hold the head in line (manual in-line stabilisation); log-roll with 3–4 people only if essential; unconscious + breathing → careful recovery position maintaining alignment
Cold pack over clothing for swelling
dont: Don't straighten, push back or 'test' the limb
Don't give food/drink (surgery likely)
topics.hospital: All suspected fractures, dislocations and spinal injuries by ambulance (spinal board/collar for spinal)

recognise: Blow to the head; headache, nausea/vomiting, dizziness, confusion, drowsiness, unequal pupils, seizure, clear fluid from nose/ear, loss of consciousness (even brief)
do: Rest; monitor response (AVPU) every 10 min; apply cold pack to bruising; control scalp bleeding with pressure
Suspect neck injury with any significant head injury — keep head still
Recovery position if unconscious and breathing
dont: No alcohol, sedatives or painkillers that mask symptoms
Don't leave alone for 24 h; don't return to work the same day after loss of consciousness
topics.hospital: Any loss of consciousness, vomiting, worsening headache, drowsiness, seizure, fluid from ears/nose, unequal pupils, blood-thinner use, or mechanism of fall > 1 m

topics.t: Eye injuries (foreign body, welding flash, penetrating)
recognise: Pain, watering, redness, light sensitivity; arc eye appears 6–12 h after unprotected welding exposure
do: Loose foreign body: don't rub; blink; flush with clean water/saline from nose outward; lift the upper lid over the lower
Embedded object/penetrating injury: do not remove or press; cover with a rigid shield/cup, cover both eyes to limit movement, lie the casualty down
Welding flash (arc eye): cool compress, dark room, eye drops only on medical advice, medical assessment
Chemical: see chemical splash — flush 20 min
dont: Don't remove embedded objects
Don't let the casualty rub
topics.hospital: Embedded objects, chemical splash, persistent pain/vision change, arc eye not settling in 24 h

recognise: Traumatic loss of finger/hand/limb
do: Control bleeding (pressure, then tourniquet if needed; note the time); treat shock; 108

Severed part: rinse gently if dirty, wrap in sterile gauze moistened with saline, seal in a plastic bag, place the bag in a container of ice-water (not directly on ice); label with name/time; send with the casualty
Partial amputation: splint in position; do not twist
dont: Don't put the part directly on ice or in water
topics.hospital: Immediately — reattachment is time-critical (hours)

recognise: Trapped under load/structure/soil; pain, swelling, numbness; risk of crush syndrome after release
do: Call 108/112; make the scene safe; if trapped < 15 min, release quickly if safe; if trapped ≥ 15 min, do not release until a medical team is present (crush syndrome can cause cardiac arrest on release)
Control bleeding; treat shock; keep warm; monitor
Give nothing by mouth; record time of entrapment
dont: Don't apply a tourniquet to a crushed limb unless catastrophic bleeding
topics.hospital: Always

topics.t: High-pressure injection injury (airless paint, hydraulic fluid, grease gun)
recognise: Small puncture wound, often painless at first; swelling later; history of high-pressure jet
do: Treat as a surgical emergency even if it looks trivial: 108/hospital immediately
Elevate; cover loosely; take the SDS of the fluid
dont: Don't squeeze, apply cold, or dismiss
topics.hospital: Always — surgical decompression within hours prevents amputation

recognise: Worker hanging in harness; faintness, nausea, numb legs after minutes
do: Rescue within 10–15 min; keep them conscious; encourage leg movement/standing in loops
After rescue: ABC; treat injuries; lay flat (HSE: no need to keep upright); monitor; spinal precautions if indicated
dont: Don't leave hanging while 'waiting for the ambulance'
topics.hospital: All suspension events

recognise: Cuts, abrasions, puncture wounds; sprain: pain/swelling at a joint; strain: muscle pain
do: Wash hands/gloves; clean the wound with running water; remove loose dirt; antiseptic; sterile dressing; record in the first-aid register
Splinters: remove with clean tweezers if protruding; otherwise leave for medical removal
Sprains: PRICE — Protect, Rest, Ice (15–20 min, wrapped), Compression, Elevation; medical if unable to bear weight or deformity
Check tetanus vaccination status for contaminated wounds (rusty metal, soil)
dont: Don't use cotton wool on open wounds
Don't apply heat in the first 48 h for sprains
topics.hospital: Deep/gaping wounds (may need stitches within 6–8 h), puncture wounds, bites, signs of infection, tetanus risk

recognise: Exhaustion: heavy sweating, cramps, headache, dizziness, nausea, pale clammy skin. Stroke (emergency): confusion, hot skin (dry or wet), temperature > 40 °C, collapse, seizures
do: Move to shade/cool area; lie down; loosen clothing
Exhaustion: cool with water spray/fanning, cold packs; sips of water/ORS; rest; no return to work that day
Stroke: call 108; cool aggressively — immersion in cool water or continuous dousing with fanning; ice packs to neck, armpits, groin; recovery position if unconscious
dont: Don't give fluids to a confused/unconscious casualty
Don't give salt tablets
topics.hospital: Any heat stroke; heat exhaustion not improving in 30 min

recognise: Shivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness after cold water immersion, cold storage, high altitude
do: Move to shelter; remove wet clothing; insulate (blankets, foil) incl. head; warm the trunk gradually
Conscious: warm sweet drinks; handle gently (rough handling can trigger arrhythmia)
CPR if not breathing — continue for longer than usual
dont: No alcohol; no direct heat (hot water bottles on skin); don't rub limbs
topics.hospital: Moderate/severe cases

recognise: Rescued from water; not breathing or coughing/breathless
do: Rescue safely (reach, throw, boat); remove from water, keep horizontal if possible
Not breathing: 5 initial rescue breaths, then CPR 30:2; AED (dry chest first)
Breathing: recovery position; remove wet clothing; warm
Hospital for all submersion victims (secondary drowning hours later)
dont: Don't try to drain water from the lungs
Don't do abdominal thrusts
topics.hospital: Always

recognise: Fang marks, pain/swelling (viper); drooping eyelids, difficulty swallowing/breathing, blurred vision (cobra/krait); bleeding from gums (viper); dark urine
do: R.I.G.H.T.: Reassure; Immobilise the limb with a splint and keep still (as for a fracture); Get to hospital with antivenom by 108; Tell the doctor the symptoms and time
Remove rings/tight items; keep the limb below heart level; carry the casualty — don't let them walk
Monitor breathing; support ventilation (bag-valve mask) if trained and breathing fails
dont: No tourniquet, cutting, sucking, ice, electric shock, herbal pastes, alcohol
Don't waste time catching the snake
topics.hospital: Always — antivenom only in hospital; even painless bites (krait) can be fatal

recognise: Local pain/swelling; scorpion red flags: profuse sweating, vomiting, rapid heart rate, breathlessness, priapism; multiple bee stings → systemic reaction
do: Remove bee stings by scraping (card/nail); cold pack 10–15 min; elevate; antihistamine/paracetamol per OHC
Scorpion: cold pack, immobilise, hospital — doctor may give prazosin; monitor breathing
Watch for anaphylaxis — see anaphylaxis
dont: Don't squeeze stings
Don't apply tourniquets
topics.hospital: Scorpion with systemic signs; > 10 bee stings; stings in mouth/throat; any anaphylaxis

recognise: Bite, scratch or lick on broken skin by dog, cat, monkey, bat, cattle
do: Wash the wound with soap and running water for 15 min; apply povidone-iodine
Cover loosely; do not suture
Hospital the same day for rabies post-exposure vaccination ± immunoglobulin (category II/III) and tetanus
dont: Don't delay PEP — rabies is 100% fatal once symptoms start
Don't apply chilli, lime or herbal remedies
topics.hospital: Always

topics.t: Chemical inhalation (chlorine, ammonia, CO, H2S, solvent, smoke)
recognise: Coughing, breathlessness, chest tightness, burning eyes/throat, headache, dizziness, confusion, collapse
do: Rescuer safety first: SCBA for H2S/unknown atmospheres; otherwise move the casualty to fresh air upwind
Sit upright if breathing is difficult; loosen clothing; oxygen if trained and available
Not breathing: CPR with a barrier device (avoid mouth-to-mouth for cyanide/pesticides); AED
Eye/skin exposure: flush
CO: 100% oxygen; hospital even if recovered (delayed effects); chlorine/NOx/phosgene: observe 24–48 h for delayed lung oedema
dont: Don't enter a confined space or gas cloud without BA
topics.hospital: All significant inhalations; take the SDS

recognise: History of swallowing chemical; burns around mouth; vomiting; drowsiness; odour
do: Call 108 and the National Poisons Information Centre (AIIMS 1800-116-117); identify the substance (SDS/label, container)
Conscious: rinse the mouth, spit out; do not induce vomiting; small sips of water only if advised
Unconscious: recovery position; CPR with barrier if needed
Pesticide (organophosphate) on skin/clothes: remove clothing, wash with soap and water; rescuer gloves
dont: Don't induce vomiting (especially corrosives, solvents)
Don't give milk/charcoal unless advised by the poison centre
topics.hospital: Always

recognise: Wheeze, cough, tight chest, difficulty speaking, blue lips (severe)
do: Sit upright, lean forward slightly; calm reassurance
Help use their reliever inhaler (blue): 1 puff every 30–60 s up to 10 puffs, with spacer if available
Call 108 if no improvement after 10 puffs, worsening, or unable to speak; repeat inhaler while waiting
dont: Don't lie them flat
topics.hospital: Severe or not improving

recognise: Sudden collapse with jerking, stiffness, frothing, incontinence; confusion afterwards
do: Protect from injury: clear space, cushion the head, loosen tight clothing; time the seizure
After jerking stops: recovery position; check breathing; stay until fully recovered
Call 108 if first seizure, lasts > 5 min, repeats, injury, in water, pregnancy, or does not recover in 10 min
dont: Don't restrain; don't put anything in the mouth; don't give drink until fully alert
topics.hospital: As above; employees with epilepsy need fitness review for safety-critical tasks

recognise: Known diabetic; sweating, trembling, hunger, confusion, aggression, drowsiness
do: Conscious and able to swallow: sugar — glucose tablets, sweet drink, 3–4 sweets; repeat in 10 min; then a snack
Unconscious: recovery position; nothing by mouth; call 108
Glucagon injection if available and trained
dont: No food/drink if unconscious
topics.hospital: If not recovering in 15 min or unconscious

recognise: Brief loss of consciousness, pale, after standing long in heat/crowd
do: Lie flat, raise legs; fresh air; loosen clothing; check for injuries from the fall
Sit up slowly after recovery; fluids; rest
dont: Don't let them stand quickly
topics.hospital: Not recovering in 2 min, repeated episodes, chest pain, injury, or history of heart disease

recognise: Bleeding from nose; knocked-out tooth
do: Nosebleed: sit, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 min; cold pack on bridge; no sniffing/blowing for hours
Knocked-out adult tooth: hold by the crown, rinse (don't scrub), re-insert if possible or keep in milk; dentist within 1 h
Foreign body in ear/nose: don't probe; medical
dont: Don't tilt the head back for a nosebleed
topics.hospital: Nosebleed > 30 min, after head injury, or on blood thinners

recognise: Collapse during storm; burns (fern pattern), ruptured eardrums, confusion
do: Safe to touch; move to shelter if the storm continues
CPR/AED first — cardiac/respiratory arrest from lightning is often reversible; multiple casualties: treat the 'dead' first (reverse triage)
Treat burns and fractures; spinal precautions if thrown
dont: Don't delay CPR
topics.hospital: Always

recognise: Puncture with used sharp; blood splash to eyes/mouth/broken skin
do: Wash with soap and running water (don't scrub); flush eyes/mouth with water; let it bleed briefly
Report immediately; medical assessment within 2 h for post-exposure prophylaxis (HIV/HBV); test source if possible
Record; review sharps disposal
dont: Don't squeeze or apply bleach to the wound
topics.hospital: Always

items: OSH Code 2020 s.24 (welfare) and Central/State rules; legacy Factories Act s.45: first-aid boxes ≥ 1 per 150 workers, each in charge of a trained person where > 150 workers; ambulance room with prescribed staff/equipment where > 500 workers

BOCW Central Rules 1998 / KA & TN BOCW Rules 2006: first-aid boxes at the site (≈ 1 per 100 workers – verify), trained first-aider per box, ambulance room where > 500 workers, ambulance/vehicle arrangement, stretcher

State Factories Rules (Karnataka 1969 / Tamil Nadu 1950): schedules listing box contents by class/size, first-aid register, OHC with factory medical officer by headcount band for hazardous units, TN Rule 63-B approved trainers (St John Ambulance, Red Cross, TN Apex Skill Development Centre for Health Care)
OSHA 1926.50 / 1910.151: trained first-aid person where no infirmary/clinic within ~3–4 min (life-threatening) / 15 min; eyewash/shower where corrosives
Certified first-aiders (St John Ambulance / Indian Red Cross / approved centre; 3-year validity, refresher) — good practice 1 per 50 workers and at least one on every shift incl. night
Names, photos and locations displayed; helmet sticker/armband
OHC: factory medical officer, nurse, dresser as per state rules; emergency drills quarterly
Hospital tie-ups: trauma, burns, poison, snakebite (antivenom stock confirmed), cardiac; travel time < 30 min; map at gate
First-aid boxes per statutory schedule (see list), green/white cross, weatherproof, sealed, inspected weekly with checklist; contents replenished

AED (recommended for ≥ 200 persons or remote sites), pocket masks, gloves, spine board with head blocks and collar, scoop stretcher, splints, burn dressings/cling film, eyewash bottles (and plumbed eyewash/shower where corrosives), ORS, ice packs, thermometer, BP monitor/pulse oximeter (OHC), oxygen (OHC)
Special antidotes where the hazard exists: calcium gluconate gel (HF), cyanide kit (hydroxocobalamin), atropine (organophosphate – medical use), chlorine/ammonia first-aid oxygen
Transport: ambulance (own/tie-up ≤ 15 min) or dedicated vehicle with driver on every shift; communication (radio/phone list)

programme.h: Box contents (typical statutory list – check your state schedule)
items: Sterile dressings: small, medium, large (6/6/6); sterile eye pads (6); triangular bandages (6); roller bandages 5 cm & 10 cm; adhesive dressings/band-aids (24+); safety pins; scissors; tweezers; disposable gloves (12 pairs); CPR face shield

Antiseptic solution/wipes; burn dressings/gel; cling film; cotton wool (not for open wounds); crepe bandage; eye wash (sterile saline 500 ml ×2); ORS sachets; sling; splints; cold pack; thermometer; torch; first-aid guidance card; register and pen
Not in box (OHC/doctor only): oral medicines beyond paracetamol/antacid per policy, injections, antivenom
First-aid treatment register (statutory) with name, time, injury, treatment, by whom, referral
Weekly box inspection log; monthly summary to safety committee; link minor injuries to near-miss trends
Review after every serious injury: response time, equipment gaps, ambulance delay
Annual refresher drill: CPR/AED, bleeding control, spinal immobilisation, chemical eye wash, snakebite
